title: ASFBIOF01-02 Polypeptide; Exemption From the Requirement of a Pesticide Tolerance
summary:
Two key moves from the Environmental Protection Agency: Mariposa County in California has met the federal health standard for ozone by its deadline, and a new protein-based fungicide ingredient is cleared for use on food and feed without a set residue limit when used as directed.

For Mariposa County, this means recent air monitoring data show smog-forming ozone levels met the standard on time. Local residents may see health benefits associated with cleaner summer air, and state and local air agencies can point to progress. Businesses in the area could face fewer new restrictions tied to noncompliance. On the other hand, some community and environmental groups may worry that reaching the line could ease pressure to push ozone even lower, especially on hot, smoky days when air quality can still spike.

The second decision allows residues of a specific protein used to fight plant diseases to be present on food and feed without a numerical cap, as long as farmers follow the label and good practices. The agency says studies show low toxicity, quick breakdown in the environment, and a low chance of triggering allergies, so a maximum residue limit isn’t needed. Growers and packers may benefit from another tool to control crop diseases, potentially with simpler compliance and more flexibility during harvest and storage. Consumers who prefer biological crop protection might see this as a step toward more alternatives on the market. At the same time, some shoppers and advocacy groups could have concerns about newer biotech-derived ingredients on food, even when safety reviews are favorable, and may call for ongoing monitoring and clear labeling. Competing pesticide makers may also feel market pressure as biological options expand.

Both actions are now effective on their respective dates. Those who support cleaner air and more sustainable crop tools will welcome the news; those focused on stricter controls or slower adoption of new technologies may seek continued scrutiny and public transparency as these decisions play out.
